title: Research Question (Introduction)
statement_text: Is it possible to determine the computational complexity of Graph Isomorphism for $(H_1, H_2)$-free graphs for all pairs $H_1, H_2$?
context_text: A graph is $(H_1,H_2)$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H_1$ or $H_2$. $P_r$, $K_t$ are the path and complete graph on $r$, $t$ vertices, $G+H$ is the disjoint union and $sG$ the disjoint union of $s$ copies of $G$; the diamond is $\overline{2P_1+P_2}$ ($K_4$ minus an edge), the gem is $\overline{P_1+P_4}$ (a $P_4$ plus a dominating vertex), and the subdivided claw $S_{h,i,j}$ is the tree with one vertex $x$ of degree 3 and exactly three leaves, at distances $h,i,j$ from $x$. Since the class of $(\overline{H_1},\overline{H_2})$-free graphs is equivalent to that of $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs (by complementation), pairs are considered up to complementing both graphs. Graph Isomorphism is GI-complete if it is polynomially equivalent to Graph Isomorphism on general graphs. On $H$-free graphs it is polynomial-time solvable if $H$ is an induced subgraph of $P_4$ and GI-complete otherwise (Booth–Colbourn, Kratsch–Schweitzer). For pairs, Kratsch and Schweitzer initiated the classification and Schweitzer proved that only finitely many cases remain open, without specifying them. Using that Graph Isomorphism is polynomial on classes of bounded clique-width (Grohe–Schweitzer), the authors narrow the open cases to 14, then prove three polynomial and five GI-complete, leaving exactly six open pairs: $H_1=K_3$ and $H_2\in\{P_7,S_{1,2,3}\}$; $H_1=K_4$ and $H_2=S_{1,1,3}$; $H_1=\text{diamond}$ and $H_2\in\{P_1+P_2+P_3,P_1+P_5\}$; $H_1=\text{gem}$ and $H_2=P_2+P_3$.
notes: Explicitly posed as a research question in the introduction; the paper resolves all but six pairs $(H_1,H_2)$, leaving those six as the residual open cases.
paper_title: Graph Isomorphism for $(H_1,H_2)$-free Graphs: An Almost Complete Dichotomy

title: Open Question: FPT Algorithm for Graph Isomorphism Parameterized by Clique-Width
statement_text: Whether an FPT algorithm exists for Graph Isomorphism when parameterized by clique-width is still open.
context_text: The clique-width of $G$ is the minimum number of labels needed to construct $G$ using the operations: create a single vertex with some label; take the disjoint union of two labelled graphs; join every vertex with label $i$ to every vertex with label $j$ ($i\ne j$); rename label $i$ to $j$. A class has bounded clique-width if some constant bounds the clique-width of all its members. A problem is FPT (fixed-parameter tractable) with respect to a parameter $k$ if it is solvable in time $f(k)\cdot n^{O(1)}$ for some computable function $f$, and in XP if it is solvable in time $n^{f(k)}$, i.e. polynomial for each fixed $k$. Lokshtanov, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk and Saurabh gave an FPT algorithm for Graph Isomorphism parameterized by treewidth (later improved by Grohe, Neuen, Schweitzer and Wiebking). Grohe and Schweitzer proved that Graph Isomorphism parameterized by clique-width is in XP: for every constant $c$ it is polynomial-time solvable on graphs of clique-width at most $c$; Grohe and Neuen extended this to the more general Canonisation problem. Whether an FPT algorithm exists for the clique-width parameter is open.
notes: Stated as an existing open problem in the introduction without attribution to specific authors; not a formally labelled environment. PDF source — math notation appears clean for this item.

title: Open Cases: Clique-Width Classification for $(H_1,H_2)$-Free Graphs
statement_text: Does the class of $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs have bounded or unbounded clique-width when: (i) $H_1=K_3$ and $H_2\in\{P_1+S_{1,1,3},S_{1,2,3}\}$; (ii) $H_1=\text{diamond}$ and $H_2\in\{P_1+P_2+P_3,P_1+P_5\}$; (iii) $H_1=\text{gem}$ and $H_2=P_2+P_3$?
context_text: The clique-width of $G$ is the minimum number of labels needed to construct $G$ using the operations: create a single vertex with some label; take the disjoint union of two labelled graphs; join every vertex with label $i$ to every vertex with label $j$ ($i\ne j$); rename label $i$ to $j$. A class has bounded clique-width if some constant bounds the clique-width of all its members. A graph is $(H_1,H_2)$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H_1$ or $H_2$. $P_r$, $K_t$ are the path and complete graph on $r$, $t$ vertices, $G+H$ is the disjoint union and $sG$ the disjoint union of $s$ copies of $G$; the diamond is $\overline{2P_1+P_2}$ ($K_4$ minus an edge), the gem is $\overline{P_1+P_4}$ (a $P_4$ plus a dominating vertex), and the subdivided claw $S_{h,i,j}$ is the tree with one vertex $x$ of degree 3 and exactly three leaves, at distances $h,i,j$ from $x$. Since the class of $(\overline{H_1},\overline{H_2})$-free graphs is equivalent to that of $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs (by complementation), pairs are considered up to complementing both graphs. The paper continues a project classifying, for all pairs $(H_1,H_2)$, whether $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs have bounded clique-width. Schweitzer pointed out the similarity between proving unbounded clique-width and proving GI-completeness of Graph Isomorphism; accordingly, the authors' construction showing that Graph Isomorphism is GI-complete on (gem, $P_1+2P_2$)-free graphs also shows that this class has unbounded clique-width, which reduces the number of open pairs (up to equivalence) from six to five, namely the five pairs listed here.
notes: Not a formally labelled problem environment; inferred from the paper's statement that five open cases for clique-width boundedness remain after their contribution. PDF source.
